statement: T.G.H. Strehlow (1908-1978), raised at Hermannsburg Mission, fluent in Arrernte, was entrusted with sacred tjurunga (Arrernte: tywerrenge) by ceremonial leader Mickey Gurra and other elders beginning May 1933 as traditional custodianship structures were breaking down — amassing ~700 largely secret-sacred objects, 15 km of film, 7,000 slides, thousands of pages of genealogies/myths, and 42 diaries. In March 1978, the German magazine Stern published a 16-page spread with photographs of secret-sacred Arrernte ceremonies, using color slides and black-and-white photographs Strehlow had supplied — despite an agreement restricting further distribution, which was violated. This publication discredited Strehlow; he died two months later, 3 October 1978. Barry Hill, Broken Song: T.G.H. Strehlow and Aboriginal Possession (Knopf/Vintage Australia, 2002), pp. 741-752, is the definitive scholarly account. The collection passed to his second wife, was disputed for years, and was eventually acquired by the Northern Territory Government, leading to the Strehlow Research Centre; a 2005 amendment to the Strehlow Research Centre Act enabled repatriation to identifiable custodians, an ongoing, only partially resolved process.
